Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

distinct adjective

separate, clearly different

also distinctly, distinction, separate (from one another), clearly different, quite distinct

classical

Cic. Rep. 2.42 (Lewis & Short’s chapter): concentus ex distīnctīs sonīs
Cic. Rep. 1.27 (Lewis & Short’s chapter): distīnctōs dignitātis gradūs

distīnctus, distīncta, distīnctum

declension

separate, distinct

The participle of distinguō: marked off, separate, each by itself; its other common sense is “adorned, set off with” (pōcula gemmīs distīncta, Cic.). The vowel before -nct- is long by the house rule; Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked.

Other words

  • proprius, propria, proprium — its own, peculiar to it

    declension · also used · classical · Varr. in Non. 361.25: virtūtem propriam mortālibus fēcit (Lewis & Short)

    Distinct in being one’s own and no one else’s (opposed to commūnis): proprium hujus generis, a feature peculiar to this kind.

  • aliud atque aliud — one thing and another; quite different things

    also used · classical

    Two things are distinct when one is aliud than the other: aliud est … aliud, “it is one thing to …, another to …” (see different).

Examples

  • Aliud est fābula, aliud rēs gesta.

    A story and a thing that really happened are quite distinct.composed

See also different, separate, difference.

SourcesLewis & Short: distinguo · Lewis & Short: proprius · Lewis & Short: alius
